item.title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
item.description: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. item.title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
item.description: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. item.title: Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
item.description: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. item.title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
item.description: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. item.title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
item.description: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch.
